sources_note: Every pattern cites a page fetched during this harvest (see observability-safety.md for the full source ledger). Nothing here is reconstructed from memory; claims that could not be verified are marked low confidence.

patterns.name: observation-tree
patterns.what: Observations (LLM calls, tool calls, retrieval steps, spans, events) nest under a trace that shares one trace_id; sessions group traces. Trace-level attributes (user_id, session_id, tags, metadata) are copied onto every observation row so aggregation stays fast on one table.
patterns.why: hermes-day writes one flat ledger row per decision. Without a grouping id, a turn's gate + ctxscore + router rows cannot be read as one story and per-turn cost/latency cannot be rolled up; a tree also gives the cockpit a natural parent for score/evidence rows.
patterns.build: Add trace_id (one per session turn) and observation_id to every row emitted by hday_gate.decide / hday_ctxscore.score / hday_router.suggest, and copy turn-level attrs (session_id, mandate, cwd, model) onto each row. Extend the day-ledger command with --trace <id> and make the cockpit ledger view group by trace_id (root = turn, children = lane decisions). No new store: the flat rows stay authoritative.
patterns.test: Unit (tests/test_hday_lanes.py style): rows from three lanes in one turn share trace_id and carry session_id; day-ledger --trace returns them ordered; node:vm view-model test groups 3 fixture rows under 1 trace and renders an unknown id honestly.

patterns.name: typed-scores
patterns.what: Four score data types: NUMERIC (float), CATEGORICAL (value from a predefined set), BOOLEAN (0/1), TEXT (free-form 1-500 chars). Five creation paths: LLM-as-a-judge, code evaluators, UI, annotation queues, SDK/API. TEXT scores are explicitly excluded from experiments, LLM-judge runs and score analytics because they cannot be aggregated.
patterns.why: The ledger records what happened, not whether it was good. Scores are the join between trace and evaluation, and typing them prevents the classic error of mixing free-form notes into trend lines (which is exactly how a 'pass rate' becomes meaningless).
patterns.build: Add a score row type to the ledger writer: {name, value, dataType, comment, metadata, observation_id, source}. Ship rules/score-configs.json enumerating allowed names and category sets (gate.verdict in {allow,deny,unjudged}, judge.confidence NUMERIC 0-1, evidence.present BOOLEAN). Cockpit: day-scores command plus a score column; TEXT rows render in a notes column only and are excluded from every rollup.
patterns.test: Unit: NUMERIC with a string value rejected; CATEGORICAL with an unknown category rejected; rollups skip TEXT rows; score rows never mutate the decision row they annotate; existing 267 tests still pass.

patterns.name: dataset-experiments
patterns.what: Datasets hold named items (input plus optional expected output); an experiment runs a task over a dataset with evaluators, and each run item links back to the dataset item and the run name so two runs can be compared item-by-item.
patterns.why: hermes-day's regex deny-list and judge rubric change often. Without a frozen dataset and replayed runs, a rule tweak is unfalsifiable and regressions in the gate are invisible until something bad ships.
patterns.build: runs/datasets/gate-cases.jsonl: frozen cases {action, mandate, expected_kind, expected_allow}. A day-experiment command replays the dataset through hday_gate.decide with a pluggable judge (deterministic stub or SystemOneClient), writes one experiment row per run (run name = rules version) under runs/experiments/<run>.json, and prints per-item flips plus pass-rate delta versus the recorded baseline run.
patterns.test: Replay a 10-case dataset twice with a stub judge that flips one verdict: diff must show exactly that flip and the right delta; a no-change replay shows zero flips; a missing dataset file exits non-zero with one stderr line.

patterns.name: prompt-version-labels
patterns.what: Every prompt version gets an automatic version id plus user-assigned labels used to route environments (production, staging), tenants, or experiments (prod-a/prod-b); traces record which version was used, so metrics can be attributed per version.
patterns.why: hermes-day's prompts are the gate rubric, the instincts/gotchas sections and the ctxscore disposition question. Editing them silently changes behavior; labels make a rule change an A/B that the ledger can attribute.
patterns.build: rules/registry.json mapping prompt_id to versions[] with labels; hday_prompts.load(prompt_id, label) (pure, import-safe) returns {text, version, label}; every ledger row carries prompt_version and prompt_label; day-sections shows the active label per section and day-section-set switches a label for the next turn only (never retro-labels old rows).
patterns.test: Unit: load('gate_rubric','production') and ('staging') return different versions; rows carry the version actually used; switching a label changes only subsequent rows; an unknown label raises a loud load error rather than falling back to latest.

patterns.name: events-only-scores
patterns.what: In Langfuse v4 events_only deployments the legacy endpoints (/api/public/traces, /sessions, /scores v1, /metrics) 404. Scores still work through exactly two routes: POST /api/public/ingestion with score-create events, and GET /api/public/v3/scores. Ingestion is queued (rows appear after ~5-20s), so a single read after a 207 looks like a silent drop.
patterns.why: hermes-day already runs this against a self-hosted Langfuse (see the langfuse-events-only-scores skill and scripts/langfuse_scores.py): per-case BOOLEAN scores, per-gate pass-rate NUMERIC, one overall BOOLEAN. The transferable discipline is idempotent score ids plus a poll-with-deadline read.
patterns.build: Vendor the client shape into hday_scores.py (stdlib only, cron-safe): push_scores(rows, run_key) builds uuid5(NAMESPACE, run_key|name) ids, encodes BOOLEAN as 1/0, posts one ingestion batch, then --verify polls v3/scores with a deadline. Score names are stable across runs; the date lives only in run_key/metadata so a trend line exists.
patterns.test: Unit with a fake transport: re-sending the same run_key yields identical ids (row count unchanged); a 207 with errors raises non-zero exit with one stderr line; verify polls until the deadline then fails loudly instead of reporting success.

patterns.name: experiment-loop
patterns.what: The evaluation loop: run evaluations repeatedly, change exactly one variable per experiment (prompt, model, parameters, scorer), account for nondeterminism, keep the baseline current, and segment results by metadata. Multiple simultaneous changes make results uninterpretable.
patterns.why: hermes-day changes several knobs at once (risk thresholds, rubric text, model). The one-variable rule is what turns 'seems better' into an attributable delta and makes a regex deny-list regression visible instead of mysterious.
patterns.build: day-loop command: freeze dataset, run baseline, change exactly one variable (e.g. RISK_THRESHOLD), re-run, print per-item diff plus summary. It refuses (exit 2) when more than one variable differs from the recorded baseline manifest, and appends each iteration to the ledger so the cockpit shows the loop history rather than a single number.
patterns.test: A one-variable change produces a diff report; a two-variable change is refused with exit 2; a baseline manifest hash mismatch is detected and reported; nondeterminism is surfaced by re-running the baseline twice and warning when scores differ.

patterns.name: scorer-scope
patterns.what: Scorers grade the span or trace they are attached to and are themselves logged as score spans; they can be code or LLM-judges, run alongside the task, and carry name plus metadata so results are filterable.
patterns.why: hermes-day currently judges at one level. Separating row-level scoring (this gate decision) from run-level scoring (this turn) is what lets the cockpit answer 'which lane is degrading' instead of 'something is worse'.
patterns.build: hday_scorers.py with a registry: code scorers (regex_phase_correct, evidence_present, cost_within_budget) and judge scorers (reason_quality, mandate_match), each declaring scope in {row, run}. score_row()/score_run() write score rows with scope plus scorer version; the cockpit adds a per-lane score column and a run rollup. Scope is enforced, not advisory.
patterns.test: Scoring one row leaves run aggregates unchanged; a run-scope scorer cannot attach to a row (rejected); a scorer that raises is recorded as unjudged and never breaks the turn.

patterns.name: online-scoring-rules
patterns.what: Online scoring rules run scorers on live traffic with: scope (trace or span), an idle timeout (default 30s after the last span before a trace-scoped rule fires), SQL filter criteria, and a sampling rate (percentage of matching traces). Scorer-written spans do not restart the idle timer, and a trace that receives new spans can be scored again.
patterns.why: Frozen-dataset replay is necessary but blind to new production failure modes (e.g. a fresh shell idiom that walks past the regex deny-list). Sampling plus filters keeps cost bounded while still covering all denials.
patterns.build: day-online-eval background task: select rows where kind in {deny, unjudged} OR hash(row_id) % 10 == 0; wait idle_s (default 30) so the turn has settled; run judge scorers; write score rows. Sampling rate, filters and idle are read from rules/rails.yml. A crashing scorer logs once and marks rows unjudged; it never raises into the hot path.
patterns.test: Sampling 0.0 scores only filtered rows; 1.0 scores all eligible rows; rows younger than idle_s are deferred; a trace that gains rows after scoring is re-scored; a crashing scorer leaves decision rows untouched.

patterns.name: span-type-taxonomy
patterns.what: Traces are composed of typed spans (eval, task, llm, function, tool, score, and more), each type meaning one thing (e.g. task = a unit of application logic, tool = a model-issued tool call, score = a scorer result), which is what makes a trace readable at a glance and filterable.
patterns.why: The cockpit today renders decision rows. A closed, typed vocabulary makes the 'who judged what, with which tool call' chain visible, and it is the prerequisite for attaching evaluation results to the correct node.
patterns.build: Map ledger rows onto a small closed taxonomy stored as data (rules/span-types.json): turn (root), gate.regex, gate.judge, ctxscore.judge, router.rank, tool.call, score, evidence. Every row carries span_type plus parent_id; the cockpit view-model renders type-specific badges and collapses score/evidence rows under their parent. Unknown types render as unknown, never silently coerced.
patterns.test: node:vm view-model test: a fixture ledger renders correct badges; an unknown span_type renders unknown; parent linkage nests score rows under the row they graded; a row with a missing parent falls back to the turn root.

patterns.name: span-naming
patterns.what: Span names follow a grammar: inference spans are `{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}`; agent spans are `create_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}` and `invoke_agent {gen_ai.agent.name}`; tool spans are `execute_tool {gen_ai.tool.name}`. Span kind is CLIENT for remote GenAI calls, INTERNAL for in-process tool execution.
patterns.why: A stable naming grammar is what makes a ledger greppable and aggregatable. Rows that read like semconv spans can be grouped by any backend (or by the cockpit) without a bespoke schema, and a name test catches accidental free-form drift.
patterns.build: hday_trace.py producing deterministic names per lane: `gate.decide {model}`, `ctxscore.score {model}`, `router.rank bm25`, `execute_tool {tool}`. Store operation_name, span_name and span_kind on each row; the cockpit groups by operation_name. Document the fallback for a missing model (e.g. `gate.decide unknown`) so names are never empty.
patterns.test: Grammar test over every lane: span_name matches ^[a-z_]+ \S+$; a missing model yields the documented fallback; a row with a free-form name fails the suite.

patterns.name: genai-attributes
patterns.what: A field dictionary for GenAI operations: gen_ai.operation.name (required), gen_ai.provider.name, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.response.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens/output_tokens, gen_ai.tool.name (required for tool spans), gen_ai.tool.call.id, gen_ai.tool.type, error.type. Message content attributes (gen_ai.input.messages and friends) are marked Opt-In.
patterns.why: This is the cheapest portability win available: name the same thing the same way everywhere, and cost/latency/error rollups become possible across lanes and tools. It also forces a clear split between cheap always-on metadata and opt-in content.
patterns.build: hday_semconv.py holding an explicit map from ledger row fields to semconv keys (judge calls record provider/model/token usage; tool calls record gen_ai.tool.name plus a stable gen_ai.tool.call.id = uuid5(session+turn+index); errors record error.type). Local-only fields stay under an hday.* prefix; never invent semconv keys for local concepts.
patterns.test: Unit: every emitted row maps to the attribute table with no unmapped keys; token fields are ints or absent (never the string 'unknown'); content attributes are absent by default; the map is a single dict, so a drift test fails when a lane adds an unmapped field.

patterns.name: evaluation-result-events
patterns.what: gen_ai.evaluation.result is an event carrying gen_ai.evaluation.name (required), gen_ai.evaluation.score.label (e.g. pass/fail, relevant/not_relevant) and gen_ai.evaluation.score.value, parented to the GenAI span being evaluated, or carrying gen_ai.response.id when the span id is unavailable.
patterns.why: This is the exact bridge a Jev-native repo needs: a typed judgment (noul + choice) becomes an event attached to the thing it judged, so the cockpit can show 'this decision was evaluated as correct by scorer X' without a parallel store or a schema of its own.
patterns.build: Emit evaluation-result rows from the scorer API and from every judge verdict: name = scorer name, label = categorical verdict, value = numeric score, parent = the ledger row id being evaluated (falling back to the turn id). Cockpit renders evaluation events as annotations on the decision row; the count of evaluation events equals the count of scored rows.
patterns.test: Unit: an evaluation event with neither a parent id nor gen_ai.response.id is rejected; label/value survive a ledger file round-trip; a fixture run with N scored rows yields exactly N evaluation events.

patterns.name: content-capture-optin
patterns.what: The spec separates metadata from content: message content attributes are Opt-In, and it documents uploading full content to external storage and keeping only a reference on the span (with streaming chunks handled separately).
patterns.why: The ledger holds commands, file paths and judge reasons - exactly the material that must not be sprayed into a hosted backend by default. Opt-in content with external storage is the privacy-safe default the repo's own integrity/secrets tests already gesture at.
patterns.build: Store content hashes plus a content_ref pointer by default (hday_manifest already computes sha1_10); a --capture-content flag (off by default) writes full text into a local blob dir and records only the ref; a redaction pass strips secret-shaped strings before any hosted push, reusing the patterns in tests/test_integrity_and_secrets.py.
patterns.test: Default run contains no command text in the ledger (refs only); with the flag the blob exists and the ref resolves to identical bytes; a seeded AWS-key-shaped string never appears in a pushed payload.

patterns.name: genai-metrics
patterns.what: Standard instruments: gen_ai.client.operation.duration (histogram), gen_ai.client.operation.time_to_first_chunk, gen_ai.server.request.duration, gen_ai.invoke_workflow.duration, gen_ai.invoke_agent.duration / .inference_calls / .tool_calls, and gen_ai.execute_tool.duration.
patterns.why: A cockpit needs rates and distributions, not just rows: escalations per minute, judge latency p50/p95, tool calls per turn. These are the standard names for exactly those rollups, and they make a later OTLP export a config change rather than a rewrite.
patterns.build: hday_metrics.py computing rollups over the ledger: gate.decisions by kind (counter), gate.escalation_rate, judge.duration histogram (ms, documented buckets), tool.calls per turn. Expose via a day-metrics command consumed by the ops-shell panel; window and buckets come from config.
patterns.test: Bucket boundaries are deterministic for a fixture ledger; an empty ledger yields zeros rather than errors; a malformed row (missing ms) is skipped and counted in a skipped field instead of skewing the histogram.

patterns.name: swe-bench-verified
patterns.what: SWE-bench scores a patch by running the repository's own tests (execution-based, not text similarity): 2,294 real GitHub issues across 12 Python repos in the original set. SWE-bench Verified is a 500-sample subset screened by human annotators for well-specified issues and appropriately scoped tests, with easy (196 sub-15-minute) and hard (45 over-one-hour) slices; OpenAI and the SWE-bench authors shipped a containerized Docker evaluation harness.
patterns.why: It is the canonical answer to 'did the change actually work': real tasks, real tests, human-validated subset, difficulty slices. hermes-day's completion gate makes the same claim with weaker evidence, so the transferable part is the evidence standard, not the benchmark itself.
patterns.build: Give every rule/instinct a machine-checkable task card: {workspace fixture, action, fail_to_pass check, pass_to_pass set}. day-suite runs the cards in a sandboxed workspace and reports per-card pass/fail plus any pass-to-pass regressions the action introduced. Difficulty labels (fast <15 min vs slow) decide what runs per commit versus nightly.
patterns.test: The suite is its own test: a card whose action is reverted must fail its fail-to-pass check; an unrelated card must still pass (no collateral); a deliberately broken gate rule must be caught by at least one card, or the card set is provably too weak.

patterns.name: tau-bench-passk
patterns.what: tau-bench emulates dynamic conversations between a simulated user and an agent with domain APIs and policy guidelines; success is scored by comparing the final database state against the annotated goal state, and pass^k measures the probability that all k independent trials succeed (reliability), not the average. Reported: gpt-4o succeeded on under 50% of tasks and pass^8 under 25% in retail.
patterns.why: hermes-day's gate is judge-dependent and therefore stochastic: a rule that passes 8 of 10 turns is not a safe rule. pass^k is the right metric for a permission gate, and state comparison is the right way to score side effects rather than prose.
patterns.build: day-reliability command: for a scenario card (action + mandate + expected verdict + expected side effects), run k trials (default 4, configurable) with the live judge, compare final observable state (git refs, file hashes, ledger rows) to the expected state, and record pass^k as a score on the scenario. Cards with pass^k < 1 surface in the cockpit as unreliable rules.
patterns.test: With a stub judge that answers correctly with probability p: pass^k is exactly 1 for p=1 and 0 for p=0, and strictly below 1 for a flaky stub; a scenario with a correct verdict but a missing side effect is still scored as a failure.

patterns.name: gaia-levels
patterns.what: GAIA is 466 real-world questions requiring reasoning, multi-modality, browsing and tool use, with unambiguous answers scored exactly; human respondents scored 92% versus 15% for GPT-4 with plugins, and answers to 300 questions are withheld to power a leaderboard.
patterns.why: The transferable design is the task contract: unambiguous expected answers, difficulty tiers, and a private holdout. Ops tasks graded that way can be re-checked honestly instead of relying on the agent's own narrative summary.
patterns.build: A tiered ops task set under runs/tasks/: tier-1 single-tool (answer a fact from a panel command), tier-2 multi-step (diagnose and fix a seeded breakage), tier-3 long-horizon (multi-turn mission). Every task declares an exact expected answer or state; roughly 30% of tasks are held out of the repo and used only for periodic honest re-checks.
patterns.test: Harness lint: every task file has an exact expected answer and a tier (free-text expectations fail lint); the repo suite never reads holdout files (path guard test); scoring is exact-match with a stated pass bar, no fuzzy matching.

patterns.name: webarena-functional-validators
patterns.what: WebArena builds a highly realistic and reproducible self-hosted environment (fully functional websites across e-commerce, forum, collaborative development and content management, plus tools and knowledge bases) and evaluates the functional correctness of task completion rather than text similarity.
patterns.why: The cockpit asserts states ('service up', 'gate passed'). Validators that check the observable system state are strictly stronger than parsing the agent's report, and reproducibility is what makes a failure debuggable instead of anecdotal.
patterns.build: Validators per ops action, declared next to the task card: git ref exists and matches the workspace hash; file content equals expected; a ledger row with the expected kind is present; a panel command returns the expected JSON shape. day-verify runs validators instead of trusting text, and a failed validator blocks the 'verified' claim.
patterns.test: Negative controls are mandatory: each validator must fail when the underlying state is absent and pass after the action is applied in a tmp workspace; a validator that returns truthy for an empty state is rejected in review tests.

patterns.name: trajectory-evals
patterns.what: agentevals scores the agent trajectory (the list of intermediate messages and tool calls) rather than only the final answer, with LLM-as-judge trajectory evaluators that return {key, reasoning, score} (e.g. trajectory_accuracy) and exact/strict matching of tool sequences. Agent-as-a-Judge extends step-level scoring to intermediate steps.
patterns.why: hermes-day's ledger is already a trajectory (regex phase, judge, decision, evidence). Scoring only the final verdict hides the failure that matters: a right answer for the wrong reason, or a wrong tool sequence that happened to pass.
patterns.build: day-traj-eval over a ledger slice: (a) deterministic strict match of the decision/tool sequence for known scenarios, (b) a judge scorer on reason quality with a fixed rubric that must return reasoning alongside the score. Store both as evaluation-result events on the turn span. The cockpit shows trajectory score next to the verdict, so a gap between them is visible.
patterns.test: A fixture ledger with a correct verdict but a skipped evidence step scores below the pass bar in trajectory mode and above it in verdict-only mode (proving the metrics differ); a judge response without reasoning is recorded as unjudged, not scored.

patterns.name: nemo-rails-taxonomy
patterns.what: Five rail types: input rails (on user input), dialog rails (influence how the LLM is prompted), retrieval rails (on retrieved chunks in RAG), execution rails (on tool input/output), and output rails (on the generated response). A rail can reject OR alter the content (e.g. mask sensitive data, rephrase) rather than only block.
patterns.why: hermes-day's hooks already line up with this taxonomy (pre_llm_call = input, ctxscore = retrieval, pre_tool_call = execution, post_tool_call = output). Naming the rails buys a shared vocabulary, and 'alter' provides a middle path between allow and deny - e.g. redact a secret out of a command instead of blocking the whole turn.
patterns.build: hday_rails.py mapping the taxonomy to hook points, with rail_action in {allow, deny, alter}; an alter rail records before/after hashes plus the reason as a ledger row (never a silent rewrite). Document the mapping in the README so new hooks land in the correct rail and the taxonomy does not drift.
patterns.test: Unit: every registered rail declares type and action; an alter rail records both hashes and the diff reason; an unknown rail type fails registration loudly; a rail that raises fails open with an unjudged row.

patterns.name: self-check-rail
patterns.what: NeMo configurations can enable self-check output rails using the application's own LLM - the README's example config lists `self check facts` and `self check hallucination` as output flows alongside moderation and sensitive-data masking with entity lists.
patterns.why: hermes-day's completion gate asserts 'verified' from evidence rows. A self-check rail that re-reads each claim against the recorded evidence (exit codes, file hashes, test output) targets the exact failure the repo exists to prevent: an overclaimed completion that no regex can catch.
patterns.build: hday_selfcheck.py: before the gate settles a pass, collect the turn's evidence rows and ask the judge a typed question per claim ('does evidence X support claim Y?') using noul plus a choice; unsupported claims force the verdict to unjudged/deny with a reason naming the claim. Bounded to N claims per turn, fail-open loudly.
patterns.test: With a stub judge: a claim with no matching evidence is rejected; a claim with matching evidence passes; partial judge answers leave the unanswered claims marked unjudged rather than assumed true; the bound is enforced (claim N+1 is reported as unchecked).

patterns.name: validator-chain-onfail
patterns.what: Guardrails AI composes validators into a chain with per-validator failure policy: `Guard().use(Validator, on_fail=OnFailAction.EXCEPTION)`, installable validators from a hub (regex match, competitor check, toxic language), and structured output generated from a Pydantic model.
patterns.why: Judge output is untrusted input to hermes-day. A validator chain (JSON schema, then enum, then threshold) with an explicit on_fail policy is the cheapest way to stop a malformed judgment from being treated as a verdict - and 'retry once, then fail-open-unjudged' matches the repo's existing failure policy.
patterns.build: hday_validate.py with validators [json_schema, kind_enum, confidence_range, reason_nonempty], each with a policy declared in rules/rails.yml. REASK is exactly one bounded retry to the judge; after that the row becomes unjudged (never a block). Every validation failure lands in the ledger with validator name and reason.
patterns.test: Malformed JSON triggers exactly one reask then unjudged with a reason; out-of-range confidence is rejected; a passing chain returns the parsed dict with no silent coercion; the retry counter cannot exceed 1.

patterns.name: llama-guard-taxonomy
patterns.what: Llama Guard is an LLM-based input-output safeguard that classifies both prompts (prompt classification) and model responses (response classification) against an explicit safety taxonomy, emitting a safe/unsafe decision and the violated categories; the taxonomy is customizable by prompting. Llama Guard 3 (Llama-3.1-8B) is aligned to the MLCommons hazard taxonomy, covers 8 languages, was optimized for tool-call safety (search and code interpreter), and its first-token probability can be used as an unsafe-class score with thresholding.
patterns.why: hermes-day's deny taxonomy (Test Deletion, Exit Code Laundering, Assertion Gutting...) is the same shape: categories, binary decisions, versioning. Making it explicit data, and applying it to both the attempted action and the observed result, is what turns the instincts list into a measurable system.
patterns.build: rules/taxonomy.yml: violation ids with human names, detectors (regex and/or judge), severity. Each hit emits a binary score per category plus a taxonomy_version on the row; the cockpit aggregates hits by category so a rule that fires constantly becomes visible (noise control). An optional model-classifier lane can cover categories regex cannot see (e.g. 'claims a check passed without running it').
patterns.test: Drift test: every violation id in hday_gate's regex tables exists in the taxonomy, and vice versa; a hit without a taxonomy id fails validation; category rollups match a fixture ledger; the taxonomy version is recorded on every hit row.

patterns.name: prompt-guard-injection-classifier
patterns.what: Prompt Guard is an 86M classifier trained on a large corpus of attacks that detects both explicitly malicious prompts (jailbreaks) and benign-looking data containing injected instructions; Meta recommends fine-tuning it on application-specific data and layering it with other protections. The model card is access-gated on Hugging Face (terms acceptance required).
patterns.why: hermes-day pulls untrusted text (tool output, repo files, fetched pages) into context. ctxscore decides relevance but nothing asks 'is this text trying to instruct me?'. A small local classifier is a cheap pre-filter whose verdicts are recordable as typed scores.
patterns.build: Optional hday_inject_scan.py lane: run a local classifier over chunks entering context; a flag marks the chunk hide/quarantine and writes a ledger row with lane=classifier plus the score. Content is never silently dropped - a flagged chunk is recorded and can be reviewed. Threshold lives in rules/rails.yml.
patterns.test: With a stub classifier: a flagged chunk is marked and recorded (never deleted); threshold changes are reflected in the ledger; a classifier error leaves chunks whole with an unjudged row (fail-open loudly).

patterns.name: dual-llm-quarantine
patterns.what: The dual-LLM pattern separates a privileged LLM that can call tools and see the user's instructions from a quarantined LLM that may process untrusted content but can only return symbolic values (chosen from a fixed set), never free text that the privileged LLM would treat as instructions. The 2025 design-patterns paper catalogues it among six patterns for securing agents against prompt injection.
patterns.why: hermes-day separates who decides (gate/judge) from what is read, but the judge still reads raw tool output. The dual-LLM split is the structural fix: untrusted text must never be able to issue the instruction that triggers an action, because the privileged side only ever sees a symbol.
patterns.build: Route untrusted text (tool output, file contents, fetched pages) through a quarantined call whose answer is constrained to a symbol (enum/choice/number, e.g. 'does this text instruct deleting tests? yes/no/unclear'); the privileged gate consumes only the symbol plus provenance and refers to the raw text by hash. Enforce it in hday_gate.decide: the typed phase receives symbols, never raw untrusted text.
patterns.test: Schema test: the typed phase's inputs contain no raw untrusted text; a fixture with an injected 'ignore your rules' string inside tool output cannot change the verdict when the quarantined call is stubbed to return the correct symbol; the injection attempt is recorded as a row.

patterns.name: camel-capabilities
patterns.what: CaMeL wraps the LLM in a protective system layer: it extracts control and data flows from the trusted query so untrusted data can never influence program flow, and uses capabilities to prevent exfiltration of private data over unauthorized data flows by enforcing security policies when tools are called. Reported result: 77% of AgentDojo tasks solved with provable security versus 84% for an undefended system.
patterns.why: This is the strongest published answer to 'the model is jailbreakable, so the system must not depend on the model behaving'. hermes-day's gate is already a policy layer; CaMeL shows how to make that layer enforce data-flow rules (this value may not reach that tool) rather than only intent judgments.
patterns.build: Add a capability table to the gate: each tool/action declares {required_capability, allowed_sources, egress: bool}. Values derived from private sources (env, secrets, ledger) carry a taint label and are rejected if the target action is an egress sink without an explicit capability; deny rows record the capability rule id. Start with the egress axis only (network send, git push) as the smallest useful slice.
patterns.test: A tainted value into an egress tool without capability is denied with the rule id; the same value into a local tool is allowed; a capability grant for one call does not persist to the next (no ambient authority); a control fixture without the check would allow the egress, proving the check is load-bearing.

patterns.name: control-flow-integrity
patterns.what: The design-patterns paper's family for injection-resistant agents: action-selector (the LLM only translates a prompt into a pre-defined action over untrusted data, with no feedback loop), plan-then-execute (tool outputs may return to the agent but cannot influence the choice of actions - explicitly framed as control-flow integrity), LLM map-reduce (each chunk processed in isolation with no shared state), and context-minimization (the user prompt is removed from context once it has been translated into a tool call).
patterns.why: hermes-day's pre_tool_call hook sees one action at a time with no notion of a plan, so a mid-turn injection can change the next action. Making the plan explicit and immutable after it is formed gives the gate something concrete to check, and context-minimization is the cheapest member of the family to adopt.
patterns.build: hday_plan.py: at turn start the router/gate emits a plan (ordered intended actions with their blast radii) derived from the mandate and tool groups, stored in the session ledger. During the turn, a tool call that is neither in the plan nor explainable by a plan step is flagged as a plan_deviation row and, for risky combinations, denied or escalated. Pair with context-minimization: after a mandate has been translated into plan steps, drop the raw user prompt from the judge's context.
patterns.test: A plan of [read, test] followed by an unplanned rm is flagged; a call matching a planned step is not flagged; plan deviations appear in the cockpit; read-only planned steps are never falsely denied; the prompt-removal step is asserted (judge context contains plan + symbols, not the raw prompt).

patterns.name: privilege-control-progent
patterns.what: Progent secures agents through privilege control: privilege is a security policy of symbolic rules over tool names and arguments, specifying which calls are allowed for task completion and which are blocked; every tool call is checked against the policy by a deterministic procedure enforcing least privilege; an LLM generates the initial policy from the user's task and the policy is updated dynamically as execution context evolves.
patterns.why: hermes-day's regex deny-list is a blocklist. Progent's framing is an allowlist scoped to the task, which is the difference between 'do not do these eight bad things' and 'only these calls are needed for this mandate'. It also gives the existing blast_radius axis a principled home and removes judge calls from the common path.
patterns.build: rules/policy.yml per task class: symbolic rules such as tool: terminal, allow: [read-only command patterns], deny: [rm, git push, curl]. The policy is selected or generated at turn start from the mandate, narrowed by the gate, and every decision records the policy id and matched rule id; mid-turn policy updates are explicit ledger rows, never silent.
patterns.test: A call outside the policy is denied with its rule id; a call inside it is allowed without invoking the judge (cost assertion); a policy that permits nothing denies everything (fail-closed control); policy generation from a fixture mandate is deterministic; a policy update mid-turn is recorded and cannot retroactively allow an earlier call.

patterns.name: sandbox-runtime-os-isolation
patterns.what: Anthropic's sandbox-runtime (srt) enforces filesystem, network and Unix-socket restrictions on arbitrary processes at the OS level using native primitives (sandbox-exec on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux) plus proxy-based network filtering, with a secure-by-default posture, and is explicitly aimed at sandboxing agents, local MCP servers and bash commands. Violation monitoring taps the macOS sandbox violation log (macOS-only).
patterns.why: The gate decides; the sandbox enforces. If a denial is the only barrier, one judge mistake equals one executed bad command. OS-level restrictions make the blast-radius claim true regardless of what the model or the judge does - which is the difference between a policy and a guarantee.
patterns.build: Wire srt (or bubblewrap directly on this Linux host) as the execution wrapper for terminal tool calls: default-deny filesystem outside the workspace, network allowlist through the configured proxy, no Unix sockets. The gate's blast_radius value selects the profile (local < workspace < machine < external), and every launch records the profile plus any violation in the ledger.
patterns.test: Integration: a curl to a non-allowlisted host fails inside the wrapper and is recorded; a write outside the workspace fails; an ordinary in-workspace read/test still passes (no over-restriction); violation records render in the cockpit. Note the macOS violation log is not available here - on Linux rely on bubblewrap failures plus proxy logs.

patterns.name: human-approval-gates
patterns.what: OWASP's LLM01 mitigations include 'require human approval for high-risk actions: implement human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations to prevent unauthorized actions', alongside least privilege, input/output filtering, and segregating untrusted content. LangGraph implements the mechanism as interrupt(): execution pauses at any point (dynamically, conditionally), the exact state is checkpointed, the payload surfaces to the caller, and the graph resumes with Command - the thread_id is the persistent cursor.
patterns.why: hermes-day already escalates, but when approvals are off the escalation has nowhere to go (observed in this very session: 'escalated: external blast radius ... no human approval gate is reachable ... blocked rather than auto-approved'). A durable, resumable approval step with a recorded decision is the missing half - and the recorded decision is what makes the gate auditable.
patterns.build: hday_approval.py writing approval rows {request_id, action_hash, reason, blast_radius, ttl, status in pending|approved|denied|expired|unreachable}. When no human gate is reachable, record unreachable (never a silent approval) and let policy decide (deny for external/irreversible, allow-plus-record otherwise). The cockpit escalation-matrix panel lists pending approvals with approve/deny commands; approvals expire by TTL and are bound to the action hash they were granted for.
patterns.test: An approval for action hash A cannot authorize action hash B; expiry flips pending to expired and the next matching call re-escalates; unreachable rows never become approvals; the panel resolves exactly one request id per approve command; a stale approval row cannot be replayed after TTL.
